candidate.answerReason: The sine product is positive on six intervals in (0, 1/2), with six reflected intervals in (1/2, 1). The midpoint and endpoints are excluded zeros, giving 12 disjoint domain intervals.

methods.label: Track signs on half the interval
methods.explanation:
A real logarithm requires a positive argument. Write
\[
P(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{8}\sin(k\pi x).
\]
We must count the open intervals on which \(P(x)>0\). Negative sine factors are allowed, provided their product is positive.

First use symmetry to reduce the work. For each integer \(k\),
\[
\sin(k\pi(1-x))=(-1)^{k+1}\sin(k\pi x).
\]
The eight signs multiply to \((-1)^{2+3+\cdots+9}=(-1)^{44}=1\), so \(P(1-x)=P(x)\). Also, \(P(0)=P(1/2)=P(1)=0\). Thus every positive interval in \((0,1/2)\) has a separate reflected interval in \((1/2,1)\).

A factor \(\sin(k\pi x)\) vanishes exactly when \(kx\) is an integer. Consequently, every zero in \((0,1/2)\), when written as a reduced fraction, has denominator at most 8. Listing these fractions in increasing order gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\frac18,\ \frac17,\ \frac16,\ \frac15,\ \frac14,\\
\frac27,\ \frac13,\ \frac38,\ \frac25,\ \frac37.
\end{gathered}
\]
This list is exhaustive: for each denominator from 2 through 8, take the positive numerators less than half that denominator and retain only reduced fractions.

At a reduced fraction \(p/q\), exactly those factors whose indices are multiples of \(q\) vanish. At \(1/4\), two factors vanish, with indices 4 and 8; at \(1/3\), two vanish, with indices 3 and 6. At every other listed zero, exactly one factor vanishes. Each vanishing sine changes sign as we cross its zero. Thus the product keeps its sign at \(1/4\) and \(1/3\), and changes sign at each of the other eight zeros. All zeros themselves remain excluded.

For \(0<x<1/8\), every sine factor is positive. Following the sign changes through the ordered list, the positive intervals are exactly
\[
\begin{gathered}
(0,\tfrac18),\quad(\tfrac17,\tfrac16),\\
(\tfrac15,\tfrac14),\quad(\tfrac14,\tfrac27),\\
(\tfrac38,\tfrac25),\quad(\tfrac37,\tfrac12).
\end{gathered}
\]
Between consecutive zeros, every factor has constant sign, so no further intervals can occur. Notice that the excluded zero \(1/4\) separates two positive intervals even though the product does not change sign there.

There are six intervals on this half, and symmetry gives six more. Because \(1/2\) is excluded, none join across the midpoint. Therefore \(n=6+6=\boxed{12}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
